# Saṅkiccajātaka (Ja 530)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Saṅkiccajātaka* (Ja 530) is a narrative text preserved in the Pali Jātaka collection. According to the traditional background narrative (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha related the tale while staying at Jīvaka's mango grove in connection with King Ajātasattu's murder of his father King Bimbisāra [SuttaCentral; Wu 2012]. The frame story adapts elements of the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* narrative cycle, illustrating how Ajātasattu—haunted by guilt and terrified of descent into hell after following the counsel of Devadatta—sought out the Buddha as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and found peace of mind [Wu 2012]. The story of the past reveals that the king had likewise murdered his father in a former birth [Tan 2002].
Literarily, Maurice Winternitz characterizes the core story as an *itihāsa* dialogue resembling passages from the ancient Purāṇas [Winternitz 1933]. In the verse narrative, King Brahmadatta receives his former domestic chaplain, the sage Saṅkicca, and inquires about the fate of sinners in the hereafter; in response, Saṅkicca delivers a lengthy discourse containing vivid descriptions of hells and the retribution awaiting wrongdoers [Winternitz 1933].
Passage-level parallels identified by SuttaCentral include the *Devadūta Sutta* (AN 3.36), the *Bālapaṇḍita Sutta* (MN 129), and the Majjhima Nikāya *Devadūta Sutta* (MN 130), with thematic similarities to the *Puṇṇātherīgāthā* (Thig 12.1) [SuttaCentral]. Shared verses or citations appear in the *Petavatthu* (Pv 10, Pv 19, Pv 38), the *Niddesa* (Mnd 15, Cnd 23), and the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 20.3) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus confirms these connections with close internal text-reuse matches, particularly sharing segments §18.1–19.4 with Mnd 15, Cnd 23, and Kv 20.3, as well as extensive parallels in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Petavatthu-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. Furthermore, DharmaNexus identifies cross-language parallels treating cosmological and purgatorial themes in Sanskrit, Tibetan, and Chinese texts, notably Avalokitasiṃha's *Dharmasamuccaya*, the *Lokaprajñapti*, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the *Mahāvastu-avadāna*, Nāgārjuna's *Suhṛllekha*, and the *Qishi jing* (*起世經*) [DharmaNexus].
